author: blu
body: The acquisition half of DHCP. `Dhcp.codex` builds the messages and parses the replies and says of itself "pure logic -- no I/O", which was accurate and was the whole problem: nothing in the tree ever put a DISCOVER on the wire, so every program that needed an address declared one instead. `cdx-serve` carried `10.0.2.15` and `10.0.2.2` as constants, and those are the emulator's NAT subnet, which nothing on a real LAN answers to.

author: blu
body: THE FOUR-STEP EXCHANGE IS DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK, and the two sends are separate act functions rather than one block with a conditional in a bind position. A conditional bound with `<-` performs its effect and hands back nothing, which compiles clean and reads as a failed send.

author: blu
body: THE TRANSACTION ID IS THE CALLER'S. A client that retries must reuse the xid of the exchange it is retrying and a client starting fresh must not, and this chapter cannot tell which is happening.

author: blu
body: A REFUSAL IS A LEASE THAT SAYS SO. Every failure path answers `dhcp-lease-empty`, whose `valid` is False, rather than an address the caller might use: a made-up address on a real LAN is a machine that transmits into a subnet it does not belong to.

author: blu
body: The socket is the DHCP client port talking to the server port at the broadcast address. A client has no address yet, so it sources from 0.0.0.0, which is what `dhcp-build-msg` writes into ciaddr as well.

author: blu
body: The poll is bracketed the way `UdpIO`'s and `NetIO`'s are, and for the same reason rather than for symmetry: a miss allocates the datagram it rejected, this runs to millions of misses on a quiet wire, and there is no collector. The restore does not happen on the hit path, where the lease being returned was allocated after the save.

author: blu
body: A DATAGRAM OF THE WRONG TYPE IS A MISS, not a failure. A DHCP client hears every other client's broadcast traffic on the same port, so the first reply to arrive is not necessarily an answer to this exchange.

author: blu
body: The lease as the rest of the OS wants it. `net-apply-dhcp-ack` is what turns a lease into a `NetworkConfig`, and a refused acquisition leaves the config in the state it was in rather than half-filled.

author: blu
body: A lease is a loan and half of it is the deadline to ask again. Without this a server keeps an address the LAN is entitled to reassign, and the symptom arrives long after the boot that caused it: traffic to the old address reaches whoever holds it now.

author: blu
body: IT IS BROADCAST, WHICH IS THE REBINDING FORM RATHER THAN THE RENEWING ONE, and that is a deliberate simplification rather than an oversight. Renewing unicasts to the server that granted the lease, and this stack does not retain which one that was: `NetworkConfig` keeps the gateway and the DNS server, and on plenty of networks the DHCP server is neither. Broadcasting at T1 is answered by any server holding the binding, which is a superset of the one that would answer a unicast, and it costs one broadcast frame per half-lease.

author: blu
body: A RENEWAL THAT GETS NO ANSWER KEEPS THE OLD CONFIGURATION rather than dropping to unconfigured. The lease is still valid until it expires, the caller is still entitled to serve on it, and the next pass asks again -- a client that discarded a working address because one datagram went missing would take itself off the network for the rest of the lease.

author: blu
body: THE FUEL IS THE CALLER'S and it should be small. This runs on a service loop between connections, so a renewal that polled for millions of turns would stall the thing it exists to keep serving.
